short: The tax a company saves because certain costs, mainly interest and depreciation, are deducted from profit before tax is worked out.
kid: Imagine you must put some of your sweets in the class jar each week. Sweets you already gave back to a friend who lent you some are not counted, so you put fewer in the jar. Those saved sweets are the shield.
detail: A tax shield is the reduction in tax payable that arises because an expense is tax-deductible. Interest on debt is the classic case: interest is charged before tax, so every rupee of interest cuts taxable profit by a rupee and saves tax equal to the interest times the tax rate. Depreciation creates a similar shield even though it is a non-cash charge. The interest tax shield is the main reason debt can lower a firm's weighted average cost of capital, and it sits at the heart of the Modigliani-Miller theorem with taxes and of trade-off theory. Its value depends on the firm actually having taxable profit; a loss-making company gets little or no shield. A common confusion is to think the shield makes debt free: it offsets only part of the interest, and more debt also raises the risk of financial distress.
example: Say ABC Ltd pays ₹10 crore of interest a year on ₹100 crore of debt and faces a 25% tax rate. Its annual interest tax shield is ₹10 crore × 25% = ₹2.5 crore, so the after-tax cost of that interest is only ₹7.5 crore. If the debt is permanent and the shield is discounted at the 10% cost of debt, its present value is ₹2.5 crore / 10% = ₹25 crore, which equals 25% × ₹100 crore.
formula: Interest tax shield = Interest expense × Tax rate; PV of tax shield on permanent debt = Tax rate × Debt

short: The idea that a company picks its debt level by balancing the tax savings from borrowing against the rising costs of possible financial trouble.
kid: Carrying more toys in your arms lets you play with more at once, but carry too many and they start to fall. The trick is to carry just enough so nothing drops.
detail: Trade-off theory says a firm's best capital structure is where the benefit of one more rupee of debt equals its cost. The benefit is mainly the interest tax shield; the costs are expected financial distress costs, such as bankruptcy fees, lost customers and suppliers, and managers forced to skip good projects, plus the agency costs of debt. At low leverage the tax savings dominate, so firm value rises as debt is added; beyond some point expected distress costs grow faster and value falls. The theory predicts that firms with stable cash flows and tangible assets, such as utilities, should borrow more than firms with volatile cash flows and intangible assets, such as software companies. A common confusion is to expect firms to sit exactly at their target: in practice they drift away and adjust slowly, a pattern pecking order theory tries to explain.
example: Say XYZ Ltd is worth ₹1,000 crore with no debt and pays tax at 25%. Borrowing ₹200 crore adds a tax shield worth ₹50 crore and expected distress costs of ₹10 crore, so value rises to ₹1,040 crore. Borrowing ₹500 crore instead adds a shield worth ₹125 crore but distress costs of ₹150 crore, so value falls to ₹975 crore, showing it has gone past the best mix.
formula: Value of levered firm = Value if all-equity + PV of tax shields - PV of financial distress costs

short: The idea that firms fund themselves first from their own profits, then by borrowing, and only as a last resort by selling new shares.
kid: When you want a new toy, you first use your own piggy bank. If that is not enough, you borrow from a friend. Asking someone to own half of your toy is the very last choice.
detail: Pecking order theory, set out by Stewart Myers and Nicholas Majluf in 1984, explains financing choices through information asymmetry. Managers know more about the firm's true value than outside investors, so when a firm issues new shares, investors suspect they are overpriced and mark the price down. Firms therefore rank their sources: internal accruals first, then debt (safest debt before riskier debt and hybrids), and new equity only when nothing else is available. It explains why very profitable firms often carry little debt and why share prices tend to fall when new equity issues are announced. There is no target debt ratio; leverage is simply the result of past funding needs. A common confusion is to read it as 'debt is always better than equity': the ranking comes from information costs, and young firms without profits or collateral, like many Indian start-ups, may have to issue equity anyway.
example: Say ABC Ltd needs ₹120 crore for a new plant and has ₹70 crore of retained cash. Under the pecking order it spends the ₹70 crore first, borrows the remaining ₹50 crore, and issues no new shares. Only if lenders refused would it turn to a share issue.

short: Using borrowed money to run a business, which makes the owners' gains and losses bigger compared with the money they put in themselves.
kid: If you borrow a friend's lemons to make extra lemonade, you can sell more cups. But on a rainy day you still have to give the lemons back, even if nobody buys.
detail: Financial leverage is the use of fixed-cost funding, mainly debt, in a firm's capital structure. Because interest is fixed, any change in operating profit (EBIT) produces a larger percentage change in earnings per share and return on equity. The degree of financial leverage (DFL) measures this: a DFL of 2 means a 10% rise in EBIT lifts EPS by 20%, and a 10% fall cuts it by 20%. Leverage is commonly gauged with the debt-to-equity ratio, net debt to EBITDA and interest coverage. Moderate leverage can raise returns and lower the cost of capital through the tax shield; too much raises the risk of default, as several Indian infrastructure and telecom companies found in the 2010s. A common confusion is with operating leverage, which comes from fixed operating costs such as rent and salaries rather than from debt. Together the two make up total leverage.
example: Say ABC Ltd has EBIT of ₹50 crore and interest of ₹25 crore, so DFL = 50 / (50 - 25) = 2. If EBIT rises 10% to ₹55 crore, profit before tax goes from ₹25 crore to ₹30 crore, a 20% rise, and with an unchanged tax rate and share count EPS also rises 20%.
formula: DFL = % change in EPS / % change in EBIT = EBIT / (EBIT - Interest)

short: The losses a company suffers when it struggles to repay its debts, from legal fees to lost customers, staff and business opportunities.
kid: If you owe lots of sweets and cannot give them back, other children stop swapping toys with you and you spend playtime arguing. You lose out even before you give anything back.
detail: Financial distress costs are the value lost when a firm has trouble meeting its debt obligations. Direct costs are the legal, administrative and advisory fees of insolvency proceedings; in India these arise under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, where cases can drag on for years and lenders have typically recovered well under half of their admitted claims. Indirect costs are usually larger: customers worry about after-sales support and switch, suppliers demand cash upfront, good employees leave, and managers cut R&D or pass up profitable projects to conserve cash. Distress also sharpens conflicts between shareholders and lenders. These costs are the counterweight to the tax shield in trade-off theory and help explain why firms with mostly intangible assets borrow less. A common confusion is to equate them with bankruptcy itself: the costs start as soon as default looks likely, long before any formal filing.
example: Say ABC Ltd would be worth ₹600 crore if healthy, and the market sees a 20% chance of distress that would cost ₹150 crore in lost sales, fees and staff exits. The expected distress cost is 20% × ₹150 crore = ₹30 crore, which lowers the firm's value today to ₹570 crore.
formula: Expected distress cost = Probability of distress × Cost if distress occurs

short: Raising money by selling part-ownership of a company to investors, who are not repaid but share in future profits and growth.
kid: To build a bigger lemonade stand, you let two friends help pay for it. Now the stand belongs a little to them too, and they get some of the coins it makes.
detail: Equity financing means raising capital by issuing ownership claims, such as ordinary shares, to new or existing investors. Routes include an initial public offering (IPO), follow-on offers, rights issues to existing shareholders, qualified institutional placements (QIPs) and preferential allotments for listed Indian companies, and venture capital or private equity rounds for unlisted ones. Unlike debt, equity carries no fixed repayment or interest, so it does not add default risk and gives the firm a cushion in bad years. The price is dilution: existing owners hold a smaller slice of profits and votes. Equity is also usually the most expensive source of capital, because shareholders bear the most risk and dividends are not tax-deductible. A common confusion is to call equity 'free money' because nothing must be repaid: investors expect a return, and failing to deliver it shows up in a falling share price and harder future fundraising.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 1 crore shares, all owned by its founders. It issues 25 lakh new shares at ₹200 each, raising ₹50 crore. The founders now own 1 crore out of 1.25 crore shares, or 80% of the company instead of 100%.

short: Raising money by borrowing, through loans or bonds, which must be repaid with interest on fixed dates whether or not the business does well.
kid: You borrow ten coins from your sister to buy lemons and promise to give back eleven on Sunday. You must give them back even if nobody buys lemonade.
detail: Debt financing is raising funds by taking on obligations that require repayment of principal plus interest on agreed terms. Sources include bank term loans and working capital lines, non-convertible debentures and commercial paper in India, corporate bonds abroad, external commercial borrowings and loans from NBFCs. Lenders get no ownership or votes, so existing shareholders are not diluted, and because lenders take less risk and interest is tax-deductible, debt usually costs less than equity. The trade-off is fixed commitments: missed payments can trigger penalties, covenant breaches, a credit rating downgrade or insolvency proceedings. Debt is often secured against assets and may carry covenants that restrict further borrowing or dividends. A common confusion is to treat the interest rate as the full cost of borrowing: more debt also makes the firm's equity riskier, so shareholders demand higher returns, and it raises the chance of financial distress.
example: Say ABC Ltd borrows ₹40 crore at 9% a year and pays tax at 25%. Its annual interest is ₹3.6 crore, but the tax saving of ₹0.9 crore brings the after-tax cost down to ₹2.7 crore, or 6.75% of the loan.
formula: After-tax cost of debt = Interest rate × (1 - Tax rate)

short: Shares that pay a fixed yearly payout and are paid before ordinary shareholders, but usually carry no voting rights.
kid: Some friends who helped pay for the lemonade stand are promised the same few coins every week, and they get theirs first. In return, they don't get to pick the lemonade flavour.
detail: Preference shares are a hybrid of debt and equity. Holders receive a fixed dividend, usually a percentage of face value, and rank ahead of equity shareholders for dividends and for repayment if the company is wound up, but behind all creditors. Unlike interest, the dividend comes out of post-tax profit and can be skipped without triggering default. Cumulative preference shares carry unpaid dividends forward, and these arrears must be cleared before ordinary shareholders get anything; non-cumulative ones lose them. Shares may be redeemable, convertible into equity or participating. Under the Companies Act, 2013, as of 2025, Indian companies cannot issue irredeemable preference shares and must generally redeem them within 20 years. Indian start-ups widely use compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS) in venture funding rounds. A common confusion is to treat preference shares as safe like debt: they rank below all lenders and their dividends are not guaranteed.
example: Say ABC Ltd issues 10 lakh 8% cumulative preference shares of ₹100 face value, raising ₹10 crore. The annual preference dividend is ₹80 lakh. If it skips the dividend in one bad year, next year it must pay ₹1.6 crore (arrears plus the current dividend) to preference holders before ordinary shareholders receive anything.
formula: Preference dividend = Dividend rate × Face value × Number of shares; Cost of preference capital = Annual preference dividend / Net issue price

short: Money a company earns from its own business and keeps, rather than paying out, which it can spend on growth without borrowing or selling shares.
kid: You save some of the coins your lemonade stand earns in a jar. Next summer you use that jar to buy a bigger jug, without asking anyone for help.
detail: Internal accruals are the funds a firm generates from its own operations and retains, rather than raising from lenders or new shareholders. In Indian usage the term usually means retained earnings (profit after tax minus dividends) plus non-cash charges such as depreciation and amortisation, which are added back because no cash actually left the business. They are the quickest and simplest source of funding: there are no issue costs, no dilution, no covenants and no need to convince outside investors, which is why pecking order theory ranks them first. Indian companies often say a capex plan will be 'funded through a mix of debt and internal accruals'. A common confusion is to treat retained profit as free money: it belongs to shareholders, who could have received it as dividends, so it carries an opportunity cost roughly equal to the cost of equity.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns profit after tax of ₹80 crore, pays dividends of ₹20 crore and charges depreciation of ₹15 crore. Its internal accruals are ₹80 crore - ₹20 crore + ₹15 crore = ₹75 crore, available to fund capex before it needs to borrow.
formula: Internal accruals = Profit after tax - Dividends + Depreciation and amortisation

short: Reducing a company's or economy's debt compared with its equity, assets or income, by repaying borrowings or raising fresh capital.
kid: If you owe your friends lots of marbles, you can swap away a few toys or save your pocket money to pay them back. Bit by bit, you owe less.
detail: Deleveraging is the process of lowering leverage, the ratio of debt to equity, assets or earnings. A company can deleverage by using cash flow to repay loans, selling assets or business units, raising new equity through rights issues or QIPs, converting debt into equity, or simply growing earnings faster than debt. Firms do it to cut interest costs, win rating upgrades, meet covenants or regain flexibility after an acquisition spree. Many Indian corporates deleveraged through the late 2010s after the twin balance sheet problem, leaving them in stronger shape for the next investment cycle. At the level of a whole economy, households and firms cutting debt at the same time can depress spending, as in the US after 2008. A common confusion is to see all deleveraging as healthy: forced asset sales at low prices destroy value, and cutting productive investment just to repay debt can hurt long-term growth.
example: Say ABC Ltd has net debt of ₹1,200 crore and EBITDA of ₹300 crore, a net debt-to-EBITDA ratio of 4x. It sells a non-core unit for ₹450 crore and repays loans, while EBITDA falls to ₹250 crore without that unit. Net debt drops to ₹750 crore and the ratio falls to 3x.
formula: Net debt-to-EBITDA = (Total debt - Cash and equivalents) / EBITDA

short: Replacing an existing loan or bond with a new one, usually to get a lower interest rate, a longer repayment period or better terms.
kid: You promised to give back ten sweets tomorrow, but a kinder friend lends you ten sweets you can return next month. You use them to pay the first friend, and now you have more time.
detail: Refinancing means repaying existing debt with the proceeds of new debt on different terms. Companies refinance to lock in lower rates when market rates or their own credit risk fall, to push out maturities and avoid a cluster of repayments, to switch between fixed and floating rates or currencies, or to escape restrictive covenants. Individuals do the same with home loans by moving to another lender, called a balance transfer in India. Refinancing has costs, such as prepayment penalties, call premiums on bonds, arrangement fees and legal costs, which must be weighed against the interest saved. Refinancing or rollover risk is the danger that a borrower cannot replace maturing debt on acceptable terms; it pushed several Indian NBFCs into trouble after the IL&FS default in 2018 froze credit markets. A common confusion is to equate refinancing with paying down debt: the total amount owed often stays the same.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a ₹500 crore loan at 10% and refinances it with a new loan at 8.5%, paying a one-time fee of ₹5 crore. Annual interest falls from ₹50 crore to ₹42.5 crore, a saving of ₹7.5 crore, so the fee is recovered within the first year.

short: Funding a large project, such as a power plant or highway, through a separate company whose lenders are repaid only from that project's earnings.
kid: Friends lend you coins to build one big sandcastle shop. They agree to be paid back only from the shells that shop earns, not from your other toys.
detail: Project finance funds a long-lived, capital-heavy asset such as a toll road, power plant, port or refinery through a special purpose vehicle (SPV) set up only for that project. Lenders look to the project's own future cash flows and assets for repayment, with limited or no recourse to the sponsors' other businesses, which caps the sponsor's possible loss. Because the SPV has no track record, risks are shared out through contracts such as construction deals, power purchase agreements and government concessions. Debt often makes up 70-80% of project cost and is sized on measures such as the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR). In India it is common for highways and renewable energy. A common confusion is to equate it with an ordinary company loan for a project: in true project finance, lenders cannot chase the sponsor if the project fails, beyond any guarantees agreed.
example: Say a sponsor sets up XYZ Solar SPV to build a ₹1,000 crore solar park, funded with ₹750 crore of loans and ₹250 crore of sponsor equity. If the park generates ₹130 crore a year available for debt service against ₹100 crore of annual principal and interest due, its DSCR is 1.3x.
formula: DSCR = Cash flow available for debt service / (Principal + Interest due)

short: Getting the use of an asset, like a machine or aircraft, by paying regular rent to its owner instead of buying it outright.
kid: Instead of buying a bicycle, you give a friend a few sweets every week to ride theirs. You get to ride now, and the bike still belongs to your friend.
detail: Lease financing lets a firm (the lessee) use an asset owned by another party (the lessor) in exchange for periodic payments. A finance lease transfers substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership, often for most of the asset's life, and works much like a secured loan; an operating lease does not, leaving those risks with the lessor. Leasing conserves cash and suits assets that become obsolete fast. Indian airlines lease most of their aircraft, often through sale and leaseback deals. Since IFRS 16, and Ind AS 116 in India from April 2019, lessees must show almost all leases on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability, so leasing no longer hides borrowing from investors; lessors still classify leases as finance or operating. A common confusion is to treat lease rentals as an ordinary expense: analysts usually count lease liabilities as debt.
example: Say ABC Ltd needs a ₹10 crore machine. Instead of buying it, it signs a 5-year lease at ₹2.5 crore a year, paid at each year-end. At an 8% discount rate the present value of those payments is about ₹9.98 crore, so it records a lease liability of roughly that amount.
formula: Lease liability = Present value of future lease payments, discounted at the rate implicit in the lease or the lessee's incremental borrowing rate

short: A company's plan for how much of its profit to pay out to shareholders as dividends and how much to keep for reinvestment.
kid: When your lemonade stand makes coins, you decide how many to share with your helpers now and how many to save for more lemons. Sharing the same way every week keeps your helpers happy.
detail: Dividend policy sets the size, form and stability of payouts to shareholders. Firms choose a payout ratio and decide between cash dividends, share buybacks or both. Mature firms with steady cash flows and few growth projects, such as many PSUs and FMCG companies in India, tend to pay out heavily; fast-growing firms retain most of their profit. Modigliani and Miller argued that in perfect markets dividend policy does not change firm value, but taxes, signalling, agency problems and investor preferences make it matter in practice. John Lintner's research showed managers smooth dividends and avoid cuts, because a cut is read as bad news. Under SEBI rules as of 2025, India's top 1,000 listed companies by market value must publish a dividend distribution policy. A common confusion is to equate a high dividend with a good company: a high payout can also mean the firm lacks profitable places to invest.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns ₹200 crore and follows a 40% payout policy. It pays ₹80 crore as dividends and retains ₹120 crore. With 10 crore shares, that is a dividend of ₹8 per share.
formula: Dividend payout ratio = Dividends / Net income; Retention ratio = 1 - Dividend payout ratio

short: The idea that investors value a sure dividend today more than uncertain future gains, so paying higher dividends raises a company's share price.
kid: One sweet in your hand now feels better than a promise of two sweets later, because later they might be gone. Lots of people like getting their treat right away.
detail: Bird-in-hand theory, associated with Myron Gordon and John Lintner in the early 1960s, argues that dividends are less risky than capital gains because they arrive now, while capital gains depend on uncertain future earnings and prices. Investors therefore apply a lower required return to firms with high payouts, so raising the dividend should lift the share price. The name comes from the proverb that a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush. Modigliani and Miller called this the bird-in-hand fallacy: paying more dividends means retaining less or raising money elsewhere, while the riskiness of the business's cash flows is unchanged, so value should not move. Evidence for the theory is mixed. A common confusion is to assume it proves dividends always add value: it is one side of the dividend debate, alongside dividend irrelevance, tax-preference and signalling theories.
example: Say a share of ABC Ltd is expected to pay ₹10 next year, with dividends growing 5% a year. At a 12% required return the Gordon model values it at ₹10 / (0.12 - 0.05) = ₹142.86. Bird-in-hand theory says a higher payout could cut the required return to 11%, lifting the value to ₹10 / (0.11 - 0.05) = ₹166.67; critics reply that lower retention would also cut growth and cancel the gain.
formula: Gordon growth model: P0 = D1 / (r - g)

short: The idea that company actions, such as raising dividends, buying back shares or taking on debt, reveal managers' private views about the firm's prospects.
kid: When a friend suddenly shares lots of sweets, you guess they must have a big bag at home. What people do tells you what they know.
detail: Signalling theory explains how better-informed insiders pass information to outside investors through costly actions that are hard to fake. Because managers know more than the market, a dividend increase signals confidence that future cash flows can sustain it, while a dividend cut signals trouble; share prices typically react on announcement. Likewise, a buyback can signal that managers think the shares are undervalued, extra debt can signal confidence in future cash flows (Stephen Ross, 1977), and a new equity issue may signal that managers think the shares are overpriced. The idea builds on Michael Spence's work on job-market signalling, recognised with a Nobel Prize in 2001. A signal is credible only if it would be too costly for a weaker firm to copy. A common confusion is to read every dividend change as a signal: a cut may simply reflect a shift to buybacks or a big investment opportunity, not distress.
example: Say ABC Ltd has paid ₹5 per share for years and suddenly raises its dividend to ₹7, a 40% jump. If its share price rises from ₹400 to ₹420 on the announcement, a 5% gain, the market is reading the higher dividend as a signal of stronger future earnings.

short: When a company uses its cash to buy back its own shares from investors, reducing the number of shares in circulation.
kid: Your lemonade stand belongs to you and four friends. If you give one friend some coins to take back their part, the stand belongs to fewer of you, so each part is bigger.
detail: A share buyback returns cash to shareholders by having the company purchase its own shares, which are cancelled in India and may be held as treasury stock in some other countries. With fewer shares, each remaining share owns more of the earnings, so earnings per share (EPS) rise. Buybacks are more flexible than dividends, since investors do not expect them yearly, and can signal that management sees the stock as cheap. In India, under the Companies Act and SEBI rules as of 2025, a buyback is capped at 25% of paid-up capital plus free reserves and post-buyback debt cannot exceed twice equity; since October 2024 the amount received is taxed as dividend income in shareholders' hands. A common confusion is to think a buyback creates value by itself: higher EPS does not make the firm worth more if it simply paid out cash, and buying at inflated prices destroys value.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 10 crore shares and earns ₹500 crore, so EPS is ₹50. It buys back 1 crore shares at ₹600 each, spending ₹600 crore. If profit stays at ₹500 crore, EPS rises to ₹500 crore / 9 crore shares = about ₹55.56.
formula: EPS after buyback = Net income / (Shares outstanding - Shares repurchased)

short: The conflict that arises when the people running a company, its managers, act in their own interest rather than in the interest of its owners.
kid: You ask your big brother to sell your lemonade while you are at school. He might give free cups to his friends or nap instead of doing his best for you.
detail: An agency problem arises when one party (the agent) is hired to act for another (the principal) but has different goals and better information. In companies the classic case is managers versus shareholders: managers may build empires through value-destroying acquisitions, enjoy lavish perks, avoid risky but worthwhile projects or hoard cash. Michael Jensen and William Meckling (1976) called the resulting losses, plus the cost of monitoring and bonding managers, agency costs. Other versions pit shareholders against lenders and, common in India's promoter-led firms, controlling promoters against minority shareholders, for example through related-party transactions. Remedies include independent boards, performance-linked pay and ESOPs, debt that forces cash out of the firm, active institutional investors, takeover threats and disclosure rules such as SEBI's related-party norms. A common confusion is to assume agency problems mean fraud: most involve legal but self-serving choices.
example: Say ABC Ltd's CEO pushes through a ₹2,000 crore acquisition that adds ₹300 crore to sales but is worth only ₹1,600 crore to shareholders. The ₹400 crore of value destroyed, while the CEO gains a bigger empire and pay package, is an agency cost borne by the owners.

short: The worth a company creates for its owners, through dividends and a rising share price, by earning more than its funding costs.
kid: If your lemonade stand earns more than the lemons and cups cost, it grows and your friends' part of it becomes worth more. Making the stand worth more for everyone is the goal.
detail: Shareholder value is the economic value a company creates for its equity owners, seen over time in dividends plus share price appreciation. Shareholder wealth maximisation, meaning maximising the present value of expected future cash flows to owners, is the standard objective in corporate finance and is preferred to profit maximisation because it accounts for the timing and risk of cash flows. A firm creates value only when it earns returns above its cost of capital; growth funded at returns below that cost destroys value even as revenue and profit rise. Common measures include economic value added (EVA), total shareholder return and market value added. A common confusion is to see shareholder value as short-termism or as opposed to other stakeholders: boosting next quarter's EPS by cutting R&D usually lowers long-run value, and firms that treat customers, employees and society well tend to create more value over time.
example: Say ABC Ltd has ₹1,000 crore invested and earns a 15% return on it, while its cost of capital is 11%. It earns ₹150 crore against a capital charge of ₹110 crore, creating ₹40 crore of economic value added a year. Had it earned only 9%, its ₹90 crore profit would still be positive but would destroy ₹20 crore of value.
formula: Economic value added = NOPAT - (Invested capital × WACC)

short: How a company's leaders decide to use its money: reinvesting in the business, buying other firms, repaying debt, or returning cash to shareholders.
kid: When you get coins, you choose: buy more lemons, buy a friend's stand, pay back what you owe, or share with your helpers. Picking the best choice is the skill.
detail: Capital allocation is the set of decisions on how a firm deploys the cash it generates and raises. The main uses are organic reinvestment (capex, R&D, working capital), acquisitions, debt reduction, dividends, share buybacks and holding cash. Good allocators compare the expected return of each use with the cost of capital and with the next best alternative: for example, buying back shares when they trade below intrinsic value, or paying out cash when no project clears the hurdle rate. Warren Buffett has long stressed it as a core part of a chief executive's job, and a company's long-run returns often depend as much on it as on operating skill. Indian investors increasingly judge promoters on it, punishing unrelated diversification and rewarding disciplined payouts. A common confusion is to equate it with capital budgeting: capital budgeting evaluates individual projects, while capital allocation sets priorities across every possible use of capital.
example: Say ABC Ltd has ₹1,000 crore of free cash flow and a 12% cost of capital. It puts ₹600 crore into expansions expected to return 18%, well above that hurdle, uses ₹200 crore to repay debt and bring borrowing back to its target level, and returns ₹200 crore to shareholders through a buyback because its remaining project ideas would return only 8%.

short: The team that manages a company's cash, borrowing, investments and financial risks such as currency and interest rate swings.
kid: One careful friend looks after the lemonade stand's coin jar. They make sure there are always enough coins for lemons and keep the spare ones safe.
detail: Corporate treasury manages a company's liquidity, funding and financial risk. Its core jobs are cash management (forecasting cash needs, pooling balances, making sure bills and salaries can always be paid), raising and repaying debt, investing surplus cash safely in bank deposits, liquid mutual funds or treasury bills, and maintaining relationships with banks and rating agencies. Treasury also hedges financial risks: an Indian exporter may use forward contracts or options to protect against a stronger rupee, and a borrower may use interest rate swaps to fix the cost of a floating-rate loan. In large groups, a central treasury pools cash across subsidiaries and countries. It differs from the controller or accounting function, which records and reports transactions; treasury decides how cash is raised, held and protected. A common confusion is with a government treasury, such as the US Treasury, which manages a country's finances.
example: Say XYZ Ltd, an exporter, expects to receive $10 million in 3 months. Its treasury locks in a 3-month forward rate of, say, ₹86 per dollar. Whatever happens to the rupee, it will receive $10 million × ₹86 = ₹86 crore.

short: Managing a company's inventory, customer dues and supplier bills so it always has enough cash for day-to-day running.
kid: Your lemonade stand needs lemons in the box, coins in the jar, and friends who pay you back for cups they took. Keeping just enough of each so you never run out is the job.
detail: Working capital management covers a firm's current assets (cash, inventory, receivables) and current liabilities (payables, short-term borrowings). The aim is to hold enough liquidity to run operations smoothly without tying up excess money in idle stock or slow-paying customers. The main levers are inventory levels, credit terms offered to customers, payment terms agreed with suppliers, and short-term financing such as cash credit or working capital loans. Performance is tracked with the cash conversion cycle, the number of days between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. Many Indian FMCG companies run negative working capital because distributors pay quickly while suppliers are paid later, whereas capital goods and construction firms need large amounts. A common confusion is to think more working capital is always safer: excess inventory and receivables drag down return on capital, while too little risks stockouts and missed payments. Profitable firms can still fail if cash runs out.
example: Say ABC Ltd holds inventory for 60 days, collects from customers in 45 days and pays suppliers in 40 days. Its cash conversion cycle is 60 + 45 - 40 = 65 days. If it cuts inventory days to 45, the cycle falls to 50 days, freeing cash for other uses.
formula: Net working capital = Current assets - Current liabilities; Cash conversion cycle = Inventory days + Receivable days - Payable days

short: When a supplier lets a business buy goods now and pay later, typically within 30 to 90 days, without charging explicit interest.
kid: The shopkeeper lets you take lemons today and pay with your lemonade coins next week. It is a small favour between people who trust each other.
detail: Trade credit is short-term financing that suppliers give their business customers by allowing payment after delivery. For the buyer it appears as accounts payable; for the seller, as accounts receivable. It is a major source of short-term funding, especially for small businesses. Terms are often written as '2/10 net 30': a 2% discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days. Skipping such a discount is effectively a very expensive loan. In India, under the rules as of 2025, the MSMED Act requires buyers to pay micro and small enterprise suppliers within 15 days, or up to 45 days if agreed in writing, and income-tax Section 43B(h) denies the buyer a deduction for such dues until actually paid. A common confusion is to treat trade credit as free: its cost is often hidden in a higher price or a forgone early-payment discount.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys ₹10 lakh of goods on 2/10 net 30 terms. Paying on day 10 costs ₹9.8 lakh; paying on day 30 costs ₹10 lakh. Giving up the ₹20,000 discount to keep ₹9.8 lakh for 20 extra days implies an annual cost of about (2 / 98) × (365 / 20) = 37.2%.
formula: Cost of forgoing a cash discount = [Discount % / (100 - Discount %)] × [365 / (Credit period - Discount period)]

short: A business selling its unpaid customer invoices to a finance company at a discount, to get cash now instead of waiting for customers to pay.
kid: A friend owes you ten sweets next week. A grown-up gives you nine sweets today and collects the ten from your friend later. You get sweets now, and the grown-up keeps one for helping.
detail: Factoring is a form of receivables financing in which a firm sells its invoices to a factor, a bank or specialist finance company, which advances most of the invoice value upfront, often 75-90%, and pays the balance, less its discount charge and fees, when the customer pays. In non-recourse factoring the factor bears the risk that the customer defaults; with recourse, the seller does. Invoice or bill discounting is a close cousin in which the seller borrows against its invoices and usually keeps collecting from customers itself. It suits small suppliers selling to large buyers on long payment terms. In India, RBI-regulated TReDS platforms let MSMEs auction invoices on large buyers to banks and NBFCs, often at rates linked to the buyer's stronger credit. A common confusion is to treat every factoring deal as a loan: a true sale without recourse removes the receivable from the seller's balance sheet.
example: Say ABC Ltd has a ₹50 lakh invoice due from a large buyer in 90 days. A factor advances 80%, or ₹40 lakh, today. When the buyer pays, the factor deducts ₹1.5 lakh of discount charges and fees and remits the remaining ₹8.5 lakh, so ABC receives ₹48.5 lakh in total.

short: A setup where a bank pays a big company's suppliers early, relying on the buyer's promise to pay, and the buyer repays the bank later.
kid: A big shop owes you coins for your lemonade next month. Because everyone trusts the big shop, a helper gives you the coins today, and the shop pays the helper later.
detail: Supply chain finance (SCF), often called reverse factoring, is a buyer-led arrangement in which a bank or platform pays a large buyer's approved invoices to its suppliers early, at a discount priced on the buyer's credit rather than the supplier's. The buyer then pays the financier the full amount on the original, often extended, due date. Suppliers get cheaper, faster cash; buyers can stretch payment terms without starving suppliers. It differs from ordinary factoring, which the supplier arranges on its own credit. Indian carmakers use it widely with their vendors. Indian banks often call such programmes vendor financing, though elsewhere that term usually means a seller lending to its own customers. A common confusion is to treat SCF balances as ordinary payables: when terms are stretched far, they behave like debt, as the 2021 collapse of Greensill Capital showed, and IFRS has required extra disclosure of these arrangements since 2024.
example: Say ABC Ltd, a parts supplier, has a ₹1 crore invoice due from a large carmaker in 90 days. Through the carmaker's SCF programme, a bank pays ABC ₹98 lakh today, a 2% discount, and collects the full ₹1 crore from the carmaker on day 90.

short: A payment to shareholders that the board declares partway through the year, before the yearly accounts are done; the final dividend comes after year-end.
kid: Your lemonade stand shares a few coins with helpers halfway through summer. At the very end, once all the coins are counted, it shares some more.
detail: An interim dividend is declared by the board of directors during a financial year, usually alongside quarterly or half-yearly results, out of profits earned so far or accumulated surplus. A final dividend is recommended by the board after the year's accounts are audited and must be approved by shareholders at the annual general meeting, who can reduce it but not raise it. In India, under the Companies Act, 2013 as of 2025, any declared dividend must be paid within 30 days, and a company that has made a loss in the current year can declare an interim dividend only within limits based on its past three years' dividends. A common confusion is to read 'final' as larger or more important: it simply means the year-end payout, and the year's total dividend is the sum of interim, final and any special dividends.
example: Say ABC Ltd has 5 crore shares. It declares an interim dividend of ₹6 per share in November, and shareholders approve a final dividend of ₹9 per share at the AGM. Its total dividend for the year is ₹15 per share, a cash outflow of ₹75 crore.

short: The uncertainty in a company's operating profit that comes from its business itself, such as demand, prices and costs, before considering how it is funded.
kid: Some days lots of people buy your lemonade, and on rainy days hardly anyone does. Not knowing how many cups you will sell is the worry that comes with any stand.
detail: Business risk, or operating risk, is the variability of a firm's operating profit (EBIT) that comes from its industry and operations: swings in demand, selling prices, input costs, competition, regulation and technology. It is higher when sales are cyclical, as for steel or cement makers, and when fixed operating costs are large relative to variable costs, which is measured by operating leverage. Financial risk is different: it is the extra variability in shareholders' returns, and the added chance of default, that comes from using debt, and it is measured by financial leverage. Total risk to shareholders combines both, so firms with high business risk usually keep debt low. In valuation, unlevered (asset) beta reflects business risk alone, while levered beta adds financial risk. A common confusion is to mix up business risk with operational risk, the banking term for losses from failed processes, systems, people or fraud.
example: Say two firms each have sales of ₹100 crore and EBIT of ₹20 crore. ABC Ltd has fixed costs of ₹60 crore and variable costs of 20% of sales; XYZ Ltd has fixed costs of ₹10 crore and variable costs of 70%. If sales fall 10% to ₹90 crore, ABC's EBIT drops to ₹12 crore (down 40%) while XYZ's drops only to ₹17 crore (down 15%), so ABC carries more business risk.
formula: Degree of operating leverage = % change in EBIT / % change in sales = Contribution / EBIT

short: A situation where one side of a deal knows more than the other, such as managers knowing more about a company than outside investors.
kid: Your friend wants to swap toys, but only you know your toy car has a wobbly wheel. When one person knows a secret about the swap, the other has to be careful.
detail: Information asymmetry exists when the parties to a transaction have unequal information. George Akerlof's 1970 paper on the 'market for lemons' showed that if buyers cannot tell good used cars from bad ones, they offer only an average price, owners of good cars withdraw, and quality collapses, a problem called adverse selection. Moral hazard is the related problem of hidden actions after a contract is signed. In corporate finance, managers know more than investors, which helps explain why equity issues often lower share prices (pecking order theory), why dividends and buybacks act as signals, and why lenders demand collateral and covenants. Markets reduce asymmetry through disclosure rules, audits, credit ratings, analyst research and insider trading bans, such as SEBI's regulations in India. A common confusion is to equate it with insider trading: asymmetry is a normal market condition, while insider trading is the illegal use of unpublished price-sensitive information.
example: Say investors think ABC Ltd is equally likely to be worth ₹150 or ₹50 per share, so they will pay ₹100. Managers who know the firm is worth ₹150 refuse to issue shares at ₹100, while managers of a ₹50 firm happily sell. Knowing this, investors treat any share issue as bad news, and the price drops.

short: Greenfield means building a new facility from scratch on empty land; brownfield means expanding, upgrading or buying an existing facility.
kid: Building a brand-new sandcastle on an empty patch of beach is one way. Adding towers to a sandcastle that is already there is the other, and it is usually quicker.
detail: A greenfield investment builds new operations from the ground up, such as a new factory, refinery or airport on undeveloped land. It gives full control over design and technology but takes longer, needs land and approvals, and carries higher execution risk. A brownfield investment uses an existing site or business: adding capacity at a current plant, modernising an old facility, or buying and upgrading another company's assets. It is usually faster and cheaper, as infrastructure and permits exist, but may inherit outdated equipment, legacy liabilities or contamination. In foreign direct investment, greenfield FDI means a foreign firm setting up a new subsidiary, while brownfield FDI means acquiring or merging with an existing local company; India's FDI policy as of 2025 treats the two differently in some sectors, such as pharmaceuticals. A common confusion is to assume brownfield is always lower-risk: hidden problems in old assets can prove costly.
example: Say ABC Ltd wants 1 million tonnes a year of new cement capacity. A greenfield plant would cost ₹800 crore and take four years, while adding a line at its existing plant would cost ₹550 crore and take two years. The brownfield route saves ₹250 crore and starts earning two years sooner, unless the old site has hidden limits.
